newsitem.title: CHINA: Philippine bonds hold steady, traders sidelined.
newsitem.headline: Philippine bonds hold steady, traders sidelined.

text.p: Philippines offshore bonds traded in the secondary market were little changed in thin dealings on Friday after the central bank said it would widen the peso's trading band, traders said.
The central bank's decision effectively devalued the Philippine currency, and the peso was off 11.5 percent at 29.45 per U.S. dollar by late afternoon.
The local stock market index soared 189.99 points, or 7.57 percent, to 2,701.14, posting the biggest single-day rise in percentage terms in almost seven years.
But U.S. dollar-denominated bonds of Philippine issuers were little moved as debt traders stayed sidelined amid uncertainty over the Philippines' economic outlook.
Moody's Investors Service rates the Philippines Ba1 and Standard and Poor's Corp gives it BB-plus.
Traders said the country's sovereign Yankee Bond due in 2016 was holding steady at 202/203 basis points over comparable U.S. Treasuries on Friday.
Ba1-rated Philippine Long Distance Telephone's Yankee due in 2007 was trading at about 218 basis points over the benchmark, little changed from Thursday.
But one credit analyst at an European-based bank said PLDT is a "net gainer" from peso depreciation because 45 percent of its revenue is foreign-currency denominated.
Peso depreciation could help tighten the spread for PLDT bonds, he said.
Top-rated Metrobank's five-year floating rate certificate of deposit issue hovered at 93/94 basis points over the London Interbank Offered Rate, unchanged from Thursday.
However, one trader at a European bank noted was some scattered bargain hunting for top-grade Philippine paper.
But bankers said a "wait and see attitude" would prevail until the effects of the peso's fall became more clear.
They said peso depreciation could lead to lower domestic interest rates and spur higher economic growth.
But a weaker peso could also hurt Philippine companies with large exposure to U.S. dollars.
"For the Philippine corporate, the question now is how adequately they have matched funding," said a U.S. banker.
Gerald Baldivia, senior analyst at Peregrine Securities Philippines Inc, said he expected the peso drop to have a modest effect on Philippine banks.
"Devaluation will have neglibile impact because banks in the Philipines have been long on dollars," he said.
Economists stressed that the Philippines' situation differs markedly from that of Thailand, where companies tend to have much higher debt ratios.
Thailand effectively devalued its currency last week.
"Coporate gearing in the Philippines is less excessive than what we see in Thailand," said Anthony Chan, Chief Regional Economist, HSBC James Capel.
